# Diagnosing Cylinder 2 Misfire on a 2008 Ford Crown Vic Police Interceptor

A P0302 code indicates a misfire specifically in cylinder 2, but the diagnostic path often leads to confusion when standard isolation tests yield mixed results. In this specific case involving a 2008 Ford Crown Vic Police Interceptor with 87,000 miles and significant engine hours, the initial symptoms suggested an ignition or fuel issue, yet the underlying reality pointed toward a mechanical breach.

The diagnostic process began correctly by isolating the coil pack. Moving the coil to another cylinder confirmed that the fault was not within the ignition module itself, as the code remained pinned to cylinder 2. This is a classic step in ruling out the ignition control module. Similarly, verifying that all fuel injectors received power and were pulsing normally via a noid light, alongside checking for consistent resistance (13.3 ohms across the bank), effectively ruled out a complete open or short circuit in the injector coil.

However, the most critical data point emerged during the compression test. Cylinder 2 showed a dramatic drop to 40 PSI compared to the healthy 125â130 PSI of the other cylinders. A common pitfall in engine diagnostics is assuming low compression automatically means a blown head gasket. The user added oil and re-tested, finding no change in compression. While this specific test often helps identify worn piston rings or cylinder wall scoring, it does not definitively rule out a head gasket failure if the leak path is restricted to combustion gases entering the cooling system under pressure rather than creating an immediate vacuum loss.

The leak-down test provided the definitive clue: a very faint hissing sound from the oil filler cap with no bubbles in the coolant and no exhaust hiss. This specific behaviorâcompression leaking into the crankcaseâis highly indicative of a cracked piston or a failed piston ring set that is allowing blow-by gases to escape into the PCV (Positive Crankcase Ventilation) system. If the head gasket were blown, one would typically expect bubbles in the radiator or oil contamination. The absence of coolant or oil mixing with combustion gases suggests the breach is internal to the cylinder assembly itself.

The shudder observed between 1100 and 1500 RPM at 40 MPH correlates directly with the loss of power from a non-firing cylinder. When an engine operates with one cylinder effectively disabled, the firing order becomes unbalanced, causing significant vibration in the harmonic balancer and chassis. The "rich" smell detected during the active misfire is also consistent with unburned fuel dumping into the crankcase or oil system due to the loss of compression sealing, though the user noted the CEL did not return immediately after refilling the oil, likely because the ECU temporarily reset or the condition stabilized momentarily.

The advanced diagnostic showing a timing retard of 10 degrees is an adaptive response by the PCM (Powertrain Control Module). When the engine control unit detects a misfire, it will automatically retard ignition timing to prevent catastrophic damage from unburnt fuel entering the exhaust manifold and potentially melting catalytic converters. This protective measure explains why the car felt sluggish; the computer was intentionally pulling back power to protect the drivetrain while attempting to limp the vehicle home.

Given the low compression that persists regardless of oil addition and the specific leak-down results, replacing piston rings or repairing a cracked piston is often cost-prohibitive compared to rebuilding the entire bottom end of the engine. The decision matrix here favors an engine rebuild or replacement over a simple gasket swap, as opening the block to install new rings will almost certainly reveal other internal wear consistent with the 6,100 idle hours logged on this high-mileage interceptor.
